title: Abu Bakr's cousin
hookLine: Abu Bakr stopped supporting a relative who slandered his daughter, and a verse asks him to forgive (Quran 24:22)
carry: wouldn't you love to be forgiven

cards: A household allowance, cut off. That's where this story starts. Abu Bakr, the Prophet's friend and father-in-law, had long provided for a poor relative named Mistah.
Then a rumor went round Medina accusing Abu Bakr's daughter Aisha, the Prophet's wife, of something she hadn't done. Mistah was one of the people who spread it.
When Aisha was cleared, Abu Bakr swore he would never give Mistah anything again. It sounds fair. A verse of the Qur'an asked him a question instead.

teach.b: This isn't a stranger's insult. Mistah ate at Abu Bakr's expense and used his tongue against Abu Bakr's own child.

Aisha's long account of these days, in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes her weeping through the nights before she was cleared. The oath is easy to understand. Then the verse, Qur'an chapter twenty-four, verse twenty-two.
In paraphrase: let those among you who have grace and means not swear off giving to their relatives, the poor, and those who left their homes for God's cause.
Let them pardon, and overlook. Wouldn't you love God to forgive you? And God is forgiving and merciful.
It doesn't call Mistah innocent, or ask Abu Bakr to pretend. It asks him not to let the wrong cut off the kindness. And it could simply have ordered it.

teach.h: WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN?
teach.b: Instead it turns Abu Bakr around to face his own need: wouldn't you love to be forgiven? In Aisha's account, Abu Bakr says yes, by God, he would love God to forgive him, and goes back to providing for Mistah as before.
Look back at this week: a disciple asked three times, a guard's hand taken, a village comforting another family, a verse against despair, a road out of Ta'if, no blame today.
This one looks the smallest, an allowance restored.

teach.h: WOULDN'T YOU LOVE TO BE FORGIVEN.
teach.b: It may also be the closest to ordinary family life.

how: Muslims read Qur'an 24:22 with the account of Abu Bakr and Mistah, and it is cited to encourage people not to cut off support to relatives who have wronged them.

o: a companion who defended Aisha against the rumor
the relative who spread a lie and was still provided for

games.q: Abu Bakr's cousin — tap the pairs.
p: a poor relative who spread the rumor

s: the verse declares that Mistah did nothing wrong
it doesn't. it asks Abu Bakr not to let the wrong cut off his giving.
the verse asks a question instead of only giving an order
wouldn't you love God to forgive you?

games.q: you're Abu Bakr. a relative you've long provided for helped spread a lie about your daughter. she's been cleared. what do you do?
games.why: he had sworn to stop. when the verse asked, wouldn't you love God to forgive you, he said yes, and went back to providing for Mistah.

practice: Think of one kindness you've quietly withdrawn from someone who let you down: a ride you stopped offering, a text you stopped sending, an invitation that no longer goes out.

You don't have to decide they were right; just ask the verse's question of yourself, gently, and picture handing that one kindness back. If you pray, you can bring the question to God in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Mistah. The poor relative who helped spread a lie about Aisha, and whose support was restored after a verse asked a question. Today's word.
